title: An exceptional component has an exceptional component in each nonempty specialized closure fibre
statement: Let $K$ be a separably closed [def-kun-separably-closed] field [def-weil-field] and $V\subset K$ a valuation ring with fraction field $K$: for every $a\in K^\times$, either $a$ or $a^{-1}$ lies in $V$. Assume that the prime ideals of $V$ form a finite chain, and put $T=\operatorname{Spec}V$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], with generic point $\eta=\operatorname{Spec}K$. Let $(X,D)$ be a multipointed $T$-curve with smooth $X_\eta$ and etale $D_\eta$. Assume that $X$ is normal: every local ring of $X$ is an integrally closed domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. Let $f:(Y,E)\to(X,D)$ be a semistable $\eta$-modification. Let $s\in T$, let $C\subseteq Y_s$ be an irreducible component with generic point $z$, and let $W=\overline{\{z\}}\subseteq Y$ with the reduced induced closed-subscheme structure [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-induced-closed-subscheme]. Assume that $f_Y(C)$ is a point and that $C_{\overline{\kappa(s)}}\simeq\mathbf P^1_{\overline{\kappa(s)}}$ and meets the marking and singular locus of the geometric fibre in at most two points. For every specialization $t$ of $s$ for which $W_t$ is nonempty, there exists an irreducible component $C_t$ of $Y_t$ contained in $W_t$ such that $f_Y(C_t)$ is a point, $C_t\times_{\kappa(t)}\overline{\kappa(t)}\simeq\mathbf P^1_{\overline{\kappa(t)}}$, and this geometric component meets the marking and singular locus of the geometric fibre in at most two points. Specialization means membership in the closure of the singleton. Components have their reduced induced structures. This is a statement about a prescribed nonempty fibre of the closure of one component; it does not require its image point to be closed in $X$. A multipointed curve $(X,D)$ over a scheme $T$ means flat [def-weil-flat-morphism] finitely presented [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation] morphisms $X\to T$, $D\to T$ of pure relative dimensions $1$, $0$ and a closed immersion $D\hookrightarrow X$ [def-weil-closed-immersion]; $D$ may be empty and $X$ need not be separated or proper over $T$. It is semistable if every singular point of every geometric fibre has completed local ring $\Omega[[u,v]]/(uv)$ over its algebraically closed residue field, $D\to T$ is etale [def-weil-etale-morphism], and $D$ lies in the relative smooth locus [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. For integral $T$ with generic point $\eta$, an $\eta$-modification of multipointed curves is a compatible pair $f_X:X'\to X$, $f_D:D'\to D$ of proper morphisms [def-weil-proper-morphism], each an isomorphism over a schematically dense open and on its generic fibre. A semistable such modification is stable if in each geometric fibre there is no irreducible component isomorphic to $\mathbf P^1$ that is contracted by $f_X$ and meets the union of the marking and the singular points of $X'$ in at most two points. Geometric fibres are [def-weil-geometric-fibre]; dimension is topological Krull dimension [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]; the local completion is at the maximal ideal [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion], and $\Omega[[u,v]]$ denotes the two-variable formal power series ring [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. Here an open immersion $j:U\hookrightarrow Z$ is schematically dense when $\mathcal O_Z\to j_*\mathcal O_U$ is injective.

source.place: Temkin, Lemma 4.4.4 proof AFTER the explicit replacement of the target by its normalization, printed pp. 31--32, referring to the normal-target compactification and genus argument of Lemma 4.4.2. The normality hypothesis is retained. Only the existence consequence in a nonempty specialized closure fibre is asserted. Primary PDF read online; local archival copy WANTED in report.md.

proof.text: If $t=s$, take $C_t=C$. Assume henceforth that $t$ is a strict specialization. By [lem-trf-nodal-geometric-fibres-reduced] the semistable source has geometrically reduced fibres. Its finite normalization is an $\eta$-modification by [lem-trf-valuation-curve-projective-preparation]. The base $T$ is affine, integral and normal: $V$ and each localization $V_{\mathfrak p}$ are valuation rings, hence integrally closed by the monic-equation argument written out in Step 5. So [lem-trf-geometrically-reduced-eta-normal] applies to the flat finitely presented $Y$ and makes that normalization an isomorphism. Thus $Y$ is normal. Let $M\subset X$ be the modification locus. The preparation node says $M$ is a finite set quasi-finite over $T$. The contracted component lies in $f_Y^{-1}(M)$, so its closure $W$ lies in this closed inverse image. Notice that $M$ is a subset of the TARGET, not of $Y$.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.4 specialization claim after normalization, with the compactification and Euler-characteristic method of Lemma 4.4.2, pp. 30--32; arXiv HTML 0707.3953v3 read, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Choose a component $B$ of the nonempty $W_t$. By [lem-trf-flat-fibre-component-closure-dimension], $\dim B=\dim C=1$, so $B$ is an entire component of the pure curve $Y_t$. Its irreducible image in the finite zero-dimensional set $M_t$ is one point $x$. Localize $V$ at $\mathfrak p_t$; $t$ is now closed and $x$ is closed in the localized $X$. Apply [lem-trf-valuation-curve-projective-preparation] about $x$: shrink to a normal affine neighbourhood $U$ with $x$ its only closed modification point, compactify the target, and extend the modification by the identity. The modification locus is closed in this compactification, so the closure of $C$ stays in the preserved source over $U$; no new point at infinity is added. Indeed $f_Y(C)$ generalizes $x$, hence is in $U$, and the localized modification locus consists of generalizations of $x$. The resulting proper flat finitely presented normal source has geometrically reduced fibres. Put $R=(V_{\mathfrak p_t})/(\mathfrak p_sV_{\mathfrak p_t})$ and base change to $S=\operatorname{Spec}R$. Its fraction field is $\kappa(s)$, separably closed by [lem-trf-sepclosed-valuation-geometric-components]. Write $H$ for the reduced closure of $C$ in this proper source over $S$. It is nonempty over $t$ (it contains $B$), lies in the original semistable neighbourhood, and its special fibre is contained in the original $W_t$.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.4 specialization claim after normalization, with the compactification and Euler-characteristic method of Lemma 4.4.2, pp. 30--32; arXiv HTML 0707.3953v3 read, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: The semistable neighbourhood and its marking pull back to $S$ by [lem-trf-semistable-marked-base-change]. The curve $C$ is smooth geometrically integral, since its algebraic-closure base change is $\mathbf P^1$. Apply [lem-trf-nodal-generic-component-closure] to the proper source, this component, its closure $H$, the preserved nodal neighbourhood $N$, and the original etale marking on $N$. We obtain a proper flat finitely presented integral family $H/S$ with nodal geometrically reduced fibres, all of whose components are entire components of the ambient fibre. Its boundary and marking are finite etale and their geometric point counts have a constant sum $d$. On the geometric generic fibre $H_{\bar\xi}=C_{\overline{\kappa(s)}}\simeq\mathbf P^1$, the boundary is precisely the intersection nodes with the other components: $C_{\bar\xi}$ has no self-node. Consequently the hypothesis on $C$ gives $d\leq2$. This step uses the new relative closure assertion; fibre dimension alone would not give its flatness, finite presentation or boundary conservation.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.4 specialization claim after normalization, with the compactification and Euler-characteristic method of Lemma 4.4.2, pp. 30--32; arXiv HTML 0707.3953v3 read, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Apply [lem-pc-rf-perfect-base-change] to $H\to S$ and $\mathcal O_H$. The sheaf is finitely presented over itself and flat over $S$, and the morphism is proper finitely presented by Step 3. Thus its direct image is perfect and computes fibre cohomology over every field over $S$. By [def-pc-perfect-complex], it is represented on a neighbourhood of the closed point by a bounded complex of finite projective $R$-modules; this neighbourhood is all of the local spectrum. By [lem-trf-projective-over-local-free], its terms are finite free. After tensoring with any such field, the Euler characteristic is the same alternating sum of their ranks: the ranks of the differentials cancel in the alternating cohomology sum. Hence the geometric generic and special fibres have the same Euler characteristic. On $\mathbf P^1$, [lem-sc-p1-monomial](i),(ii) at $d=0$ gives $h^0=1$ and $h^1=0$. Higher cohomology vanishes by [lem-sc-noetherian-cohomology-above-dimension]; this curve is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian]. Therefore $\chi(H_{\bar t},\mathcal O)=1$.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.4 specialization claim after normalization, with the compactification and Euler-characteristic method of Lemma 4.4.2, pp. 30--32; arXiv HTML 0707.3953v3 read, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: The valuation ring $R$ is integrally closed: for an integral $a\in\operatorname{Frac}R$ outside $R$, one has $a^{-1}\in R$, and multiplying its monic equation by $a^{-(n-1)}$ expresses $a$ as an element of $R$, a contradiction. Its localizations are valuation rings by the same criterion, so $S$ is normal integral. The source $H$ is integral and dominates $S$, and its proper geometrically integral generic fibre has global functions $\kappa(s)$ by [lem-pc-h0-proper-variety](2). Thus [lem-trf-proper-normal-geometric-connectedness] applies, including its dominance and generic-global-functions hypotheses. It makes $F=H_{\bar t}$ nonempty and connected. By Step 3, $F$ is also proper, reduced, pure one-dimensional and nodal.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.4 specialization claim after normalization, with the compactification and Euler-characteristic method of Lemma 4.4.2, pp. 30--32; arXiv HTML 0707.3953v3 read, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text:
Let $F_1,\ldots,F_v$ be the components of $F$, let $e$ count its internal nodes including self-nodes, and let $g_i$ be the genus of the normalization of $F_i$. These normalizations are smooth proper connected curves by [lem-trf-nodal-normalization-adjunction]. Apply [lem-trf-nodal-curve-normalization-euler] to the connected nodal curve $F$. Step 4 gives
$$0=(e-v+1)+\sum_i g_i.$$
The finite dual multigraph is connected. Repeatedly adjoining an edge to a vertex not yet reached constructs a spanning tree with $v-1$ edges; hence $e-v+1\geq0$. Every $g_i\geq0$, so all these terms are zero. Thus the graph is a tree, with no self-loop, and every normalized component has genus zero. By [lem-trf-genus-zero-smooth-proper-line] those normalizations are projective lines. The branch and smooth-locus clauses of [lem-trf-nodal-normalization-adjunction] say that the only singularities of a reduced component are self-nodes and its normalization is an isomorphism elsewhere. Since there are no self-nodes, each $F_i$ itself is $\mathbf P^1$.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.4 specialization claim after normalization, with the compactification and Euler-characteristic method of Lemma 4.4.2, pp. 30--32; arXiv HTML 0707.3953v3 read, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Step 3 supplies at most two external points on $F$, counting its ambient boundary and its markings. If the tree has one vertex, that component therefore has at most two special points. If there is more than one vertex, the ends of a longest simple path give two leaves. Since there are at most two external points in total, at least one leaf carries at most one of them. Choose that leaf. It has one internal node and at most one external point, hence at most two special points in the ORIGINAL geometric fibre of $Y$. There are no further ambient singular points on it: an ambient node is either an internal node of $F$ or a boundary point, and the boundary identification of Step 3 is fibrewise. Call the selected geometric component $L$.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.4 specialization claim after normalization, with the compactification and Euler-characteristic method of Lemma 4.4.2, pp. 30--32; arXiv HTML 0707.3953v3 read, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-sepclosed-valuation-geometric-components] to the geometrically reduced fibre $Y_t$, whose geometric reducedness is [lem-trf-nodal-geometric-fibres-reduced]. It supplies a component $C_t$ of $Y_t$, with reduced structure, whose algebraic-closure base change is the selected $L\simeq\mathbf P^1$. By the component and closure identifications of Steps 2--3, it lies in $W_t$. Its image is a point: $W\subset f_Y^{-1}(M)$ from Step 1, and an irreducible subset of the finite zero-dimensional fibre $M_t$ is a singleton. The geometric marking and node bound is exactly the bound for $L$ proved in Step 7. This proves all clauses without requiring that its image point be closed in the original $X$.
